known.evidence: "The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches quoted literals. For a constant like `{{ "a..b" }}`, `FilterExpression` stores the already-resolved string as `var`, so the deprecation warning fires even though no lookup happens"; fix: warn only when `var` is a `Variable` whose `lookups` contains an empty string.

other.summary: Tests only cover `{{ doubledot..lookup }}`: no negative test for literals, and double-dot in tags ({% if a..b %}, {% for %}) is neither covered nor documented in the release note
other.reason: True that the warning is only in the VAR-token branch (base.py:558) and tags go through compile_filter without it. But the missing negative test restates K1, and tag scope is a deliberate limit that won't break anything when the deprecation ends (the error is also raised only in the VAR branch). This is a test/docs nit.

known.evidence: "The deprecation warning also fires for string literals and translated strings that contain `..`"; "`FilterExpression.__init__` resolves quoted constants at parse time (`Variable(constant).resolve({})`), so `filter_expression.var` is the plain string"; mentions the -W error impact and the TemplateSyntaxError once the deprecation ends; fix: `is_var` plus `"" in var.lookups`. (Minor misstatement: claims `_("...")` stays a Variable, but it is resolved to a lazy translated string; the conclusion still holds.)

"When the expression starts with a quoted constant, `FilterExpression.__init__` stores the resolved string in `.var`, not a `Variable` (`base.py:770-773`, `self.var = var_obj` at line 799). So `{{ "Loading..." }}`, `{{ "wait.."|upper }}` and `{{ _("Please wait...") }}` all contain `..` and match"; mentions breakage once the deprecation ends; fix: check `filter_expression.is_var` or an empty entry in `.lookups`.
